Used as a selective pre- and early post-emergence herbicide in soybeans, strawberries, various vegetable crops and ornamentals. Chloroxuron is a member of the class of phenylureas that is N,N-dimethylurea in which a hydrogen of the amino group is replaced by a 4-(4-chlorophenoxy)phenyl group. It is a phenylurea herbicide used for the control of annual grasses, mosses and broad-leaved weeds. Common crop plants for which the herbicicide is useful are soy beans, onions, strawberries, and celery. It has a role as a herbicide. It is an aromatic ether, a member of phenylureas and a member of monochlorobenzenes.

StringWithMarkup.String: Signs and Symptoms of Chloroxuron Exposure: Acute exposure to chloroxuron may produce the following signs and symptoms: dilated pupils, visual disturbances, methemoglobinemia, cyanosis, chest pain, irregular heartbeat, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, dehydration, urinary retention, and urinary tract irritation. Muscular weakness, aching, tremors, mental confusion, and central nervous system depression may also be noted. Contact with chloroxuron dust may produce irritation of the eye and mucous membranes of the respiratory system.

Emergency Life-Support Procedures: Acute exposure to chloroxuron may require decontamination and life support for the victims. Emergency personnel should wear protective clothing appropriate to the type and degree of contamination. Air-purifying or supplied-air respiratory equipment should also be worn, as necessary. Rescue vehicles should carry supplies such as plastic sheeting and disposable plastic bags to assist in preventing spread of contamination.

3. Obtain authorization and/or further instructions from the local hospital for administration of an antidote or performance of other invasive procedures.
4. Transport to a health care facility.

StringWithMarkup.String: Tenoran (CAS# 1982-47-4) was evaluated for evidence of developmental toxicity. Pregnant Charles River rats (26 rats/group) were dosed with 0, 5, 25, or 125 mg/kg body weight by oral gavage on days 6-15 of gestation. No compound-related mortalities occurred during the study. At 125 mg/kg, 26/26 rats appeared pale. In the 125 and 25 mg/kg groups, treatment related enlarged spleens and a misshappened spleen were observed in 22/26 and 1/26 dams respectively. Additionally, 1/26 rats in the 25 mg/kg dose group had an enlarged and necrotic spleen. One rat with ptosis was observed at the 125 mg/kg dose. One of 26 and 2/26 rats of the 25 and 125 mg/kg dose group had hollow kidney(s). Signs of toxicity at the 125 mg/kg dose included statistically significant (p<0.05) decreased food consumption, body weight, and body weight gain. No compound-related effects on reproductive parameters examined were observed, including the number of corpora lutea, implantation sites, live fetuses, resorptions, dead fetuses, post- implantation, and post-implantation loss. At 125 mg/kg, fetal weights were significantly (p<0.05) decreased. Visceral variations were observed with a similar incidence across all dose groups and were limited to variations in the kidneys and ureters. The incidence of skeletal variations significantly (p<0.05) increased in the 125 mg/kg group and included bipartite and not- ossified vertebral centrum; wavy ribs; not completely ossified os pubis, premaxillae, parietal bones, occipitals and teeth; and not-ossified metacarpals and sternebrae. The maternal and fetal no-observable-effect-levels (NOELS) were 5 and 25 mg/kg, respectively. The maximum tolerated dose (MTD) was 125 mg/kg.

StringWithMarkup.String: Tenoran (CAS# 1982-47-4) was evaluated for reproductive toxicity in a 2-generation test. The test material was fed at dietary levels of 0, 10, 100, or 1000 ppm to Charles River rats (30/sex/group). The treatment period was continuous (7 days/week) prior to cohabitation, throughout cohabitation, gestation and lactation. There were no treatment related effects in the 10 ppm group. Minimal effects were observed in the F1 parental generation at 100 ppm including slight reductions in mean body weight gains, and the single occurrence of lesions of the spleen. In the 1000 ppm group, treatment related changes in the F0 and F1 parental generations included: clinical signs of pale eyes and/or pinnae and extremities; statistically significant (p<0.05) reduced mean body weight, body weight gain and mean food consumption; alterations in mean absolute and/or relative ovarian and/or testicular weights; enlarged spleens, characterized by congestion, hemosiderosis, and extramedullary hematopoiesis in the majority of the parental F0 females, all parental F1 females, and one parental F1 male. No remarkable gross or macroscopic findings were observed in any of the reproductive organs or the pituitary glands examined were noted in the F0, F1, and F2 generations. No treatment-related effects were noted on precoital interval, gestation duration, mating, fertility and gestation indices, mean numbers of implantation sites and viable neonates, mean calculated or percentages of post-implantation loss, mean numbers and percentages of stillbirths, F1 or F2 pup survival, pup sex ratios or pup malformations. At 1000 ppm, statistically (p<0.05) reduced mean F1 and F2 male and female pup weights throughout the postpartum period, nor were enlarged and/or darkened spleens seen in F1 weanling. The maximum tolerated dose (MTD) was achieved or exceeded at 1000 ppm, given the large reductions in body weight. The no-observable effect level (NOEL) was 10 ppm.

StringWithMarkup.String: Chloroxuron's former use as a herbicide will have resulted in its release to the environment. If released into the atmosphere, chloroxuron will exist mostly in the particulate phase in the ambient atmosphere, based on a measured vapor pressure of 3.9X10-9 mm Hg at 25 °C. A recommended Koc value of 2820 suggests that chloroxuron will have slight mobility in soil. Volatilization from moist soil is not expected based upon an estimated Henry's Law constant of 4.03X10-10 atm-cu m/mole. Volatilization from dry soil surfaces should not be important given the vapor pressure of this compound. The microorganism Polygonum convolvulus was demonstrated to metabolize chloroxuron more rapidly than Galinsoga parviflora. Aerobic degradation of chloroxuron produced N-(4-chlorophenoxy)-phenyl-N-methylurea, N-(4-chlorophenoxy)-phenylurea, and (4-chlorophenoxy)-aniline. The field dissipation half-life of chloroxuron has a recommended value of 45 days; however, values range from 30 to 60 days. The half-life of chloroxuron in silt loam soil under aerobic conditions is recommended as 110 days. In water, chloroxuron is expected to adsorb to sediment or particulate matter based on its Koc value. This compound is not expected to volatilize from water surfaces given its estimated Henry's Law constant. Bioconcentration in aquatic organisms should be high, but not very high, based upon an estimated BCF value of 295. Given the commercial uses of chloroxuron, human exposure in the past appears to have been likely from occupational situations through dermal and inhalation routes. (SRC)

Section.Description: Sorption to soils and sediments is an important factor on the transport and fate of organic contaminants in the environment.  The soil/water adsorption coefficient, also known as solid-water distribution coefficient (Kd), measures the amount of chemical substance adsorbed onto soil per amount of water.  Since adsorption occurs predominantly by partition into the soil organic matter, it is more useful to normalize the Kd value to the organic carbon content of a soil and express the distribution coefficient in Koc (organic carbon normalized distribution coefficient).  The greater the Kd (or Koc) value, the less likely a chemical will leach or contribute to runoff.  A very high value means it is strongly adsorbed onto soil and organic matter and does not move throughout the soil.
